correctness.rationale: The quotient has weight product_i (n_i)_(deg(i)) under uniform sampling of physical matchings. Contracting a prescribed index matching in the weighted Prüfer sum gives (sum_i x_i)^(k−r−2) times product_(i,j in F)(x_i+x_j); singleton factors cancel. The chosen endpoint indices are distinct, so the falling-factorial evaluation consumes one unit of capacity at each chosen endpoint and leaves (M−r)_(k−r−2) completions in the aggregate. The unrestricted evaluator is (M)_(k−2); the ratio yields the displayed probabilities, and subtraction gives the stated covariance. There are at least two contracted components, and M≥k−2≥r. Zero-weight pairs are impossible; covariance denominators are only used when k≥4. An independent derivation by contracting the physical graph is given below. The two finite test methods in the supplied script were inspected, not executed.

evidence: Theorem 11 counts all physical interconnection trees for arbitrary complete multipartite part sizes. The paper's §5 instead orders tree enumeration by additive edge costs.

The uniform complete-graph forest law in Vondrák's notes gives (2/k)^r and zero covariance for a disjoint matching; Resultary ae093623ed5f derives a uniform Cayley quotient under a different conditioning on an ordinary K_(n,n) spanning tree.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The arbitrary-profile physical count applies to the contracted instance, while uniform-Cayley or additive-cost models are not the target weighted probability law.

evidence: For each disjoint prescribed pair {i,j}, choose its actual edge in n_i n_j ways. Remove those endpoints (they cannot be reused) and merge the two residual parts into one of size w_ij=n_i+n_j−2. Between distinct merged components all surviving edges exist; within a component no edge is allowed in a completion because it would make a quotient cycle.

Completions correspond bijectively to physical interconnection trees in the residual complete multipartite graph: the edge sets are unchanged on the surviving labeled vertices, and contracting or restoring the forced forest takes quotient trees to quotient trees. There are k−r parts, total N−2r, and surplus M−r. A zero merged size makes completion impossible; with two residual parts the count is their size product, the same formula.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The prior theorem counts these completions by (M−r)_(k−r−2) times the product of the residual part sizes. Multiplying by the choices of forced edges cancels every original part-size factor in the denominator and leaves product w_ij divided by (M)_r. Covariance and the conditional formula result by one subtraction and one ratio respectively. The restricted polynomial is an alternative proof, not a needed extension of the old counting theorem.

originality.rationale: The cited prior exact counting theorem already yields this inclusion law as a direct corollary: after fixing the actual edges above the prescribed pairs, delete their used endpoints and merge the paired parts. The remaining problem is precisely another instance of the same complete multipartite interconnection-tree count, with no additional restrictions. The product, covariance and conditional law follow from that count by cancellation. This is an implication finding, not a claim that the probability display appears verbatim in the paper.
residual_risks: The search was bounded; an earlier explicit statement of the event formula was not identified. The corollary comparison does not depend on finding such a statement.

value.rationale: Positive rather than zero covariance is a useful contrast between two sampling laws. As a distinct scientific contribution, however, the proposed exact matching invariant is mechanically implied by the pre-existing arbitrary-profile count: fixing and contracting the required edges stays in exactly that class, with explicit residual capacities. The conditional and covariance readouts need no further result.
